paragraphs: §1 — The doctrine and its single foundation: infant suffering is deserved, hence from a prior round

That upon which whoever professes metempsychosis (al-tanāsukh) among the professors of [God's] unity (al-muwaḥḥida) relies is this: they have alleged that God's afflicting of infants (mighty and exalted is He) — and of those who resemble them — cannot but be either just or unjust; and the Creator (mighty and exalted) is far too exalted for injustice, since the one who acts unjustly is the one who is in need, whereas God (blessed and exalted) is self-sufficient, in no need [of anything]. So it is established that He is not unjust toward them in these afflictions. And if He is not unjust toward them, it must be that they are deserving of what He has done to them of afflictions, harm, griefs, and sorrows; and they would not be deserving of that unless they had performed deeds by which they merit it. And if that is so, it must be that they had [already] been created at some time other than this present one — the one in which they are infants — and were intelligent and full-grown (ʿuqalāʾ bālighīn); and God charged them with thanking Him and knowing Him, but they were ignorant of Him, disbelieved in Him, and did not thank Him; so He transformed them from the form in which they were created at first into this form in which we see them, and punished them with these afflictions and these griefs for their former, wicked deeds. This is a root (aṣl) upon which they are agreed, and which they adduce as their ground; then they differ, after that, in [various] doctrines they have built upon this root — whose corruption has [now] been made plain. And when the root is invalidated, all the branches (furūʿ) that branch off from it and are built upon it are [thereby] invalidated.

: The preamble states the transmigrationists' case as a single deductive chain resting on one premise. The structure is a theodicy: (a) infant suffering is real; (b) God cannot be unjust (the standard Bahshamī ground — injustice presupposes ḥāja, need, and God is ghanī, self-sufficient); (c) therefore the suffering is deserved; (d) the deserving infant cannot have earned it in this life; (e) hence a prior life of full-grown, accountable existence (ʿuqalāʾ bālighīn) in which it sinned, was disbelieving, and was punished by transmigration into the present body. Q's reply is governed by the same aṣl / farʿ (root / branch) hermeneutic that organizes Bab 6 §1 and Bab 8: invalidate the root-premise (here premise (c), that undeserved pain is eo ipso injustice) and the whole edifice of metempsychotic doctrines collapses. The adversaries are muwaḥḥida (unitarians) who err on the soul, not the Christian dualists of Babs 1–7 — an intra-monotheist target, like the resurrection-deniers of Bab 8.
§2 — The pedagogy counterexample: a father disciplines and teaches his child, who had committed no prior sin

So among that with which they are confronted in this is that it is said to them: why have you alleged that pain, when it befalls the one pained without a sin of his by which he deserved it, is injustice? Their answer in that is to say: because we found, in the observable [world] (al-shāhid) and in reason (al-maʿqūl), that one whom we pained without a crime of his against us — we have [thereby] wronged him; and likewise, were we to pain another, or strike him, without his deserving that from us by a crime of his, we would by that be wrongdoers toward him.

It is said to them: and why have you alleged that all pains follow this [same] path, and that this [holds] in the observable and the rational [world] — when the matter, in our view, is the contrary of that? Then it is said to them: inform us about one who takes his child in hand with discipline and instruction (al-taʾdīb wa-l-taʿlīm), along with what there is in that for his child of toil, and what reaches him of griefs, sorrows, and pains — without there having been any prior sin by the child for which this would be a punishment of him: do you allege that he is by that a wrongdoer toward him? If they say "yes," they have departed from reason, since they would [then] be alleging that people's disciplining of their children, and their teaching them what sets right their religion and their worldly life, is foul (qabīḥ) — when they did not intend by it their punishment.

: The first and controlling counterexample. The transmigrationists' premise rests on an induction from human cases ("whomever we pain undeservedly we wrong"); Q breaks the induction with a human case that defeats it — a parent's pedagogical discipline inflicts real pain (taʿab, ghumūm, ālām) on a child who has committed no prior sin, yet no one calls it injustice. al-taʾdīb wa-l-taʿlīm (discipline and instruction) is the paradigm of beneficial, non-punitive, undeserved pain. To deny it is qabīḥ (foul) is to "depart from reason" (kharajū min al-maʿqūl) — the Bahshamī appeal to universal moral intuition that Q shares.
§3 — Extended to medicine, and to self-imposed toil in the pursuit of knowledge

So it is said to them: then likewise it must also follow that, when they pain them by cupping (al-ḥijāma), bloodletting (al-faṣd), the drinking of medicine, and by that with which they treat their eyes in ophthalmia (al-ramad) and the like — [it must follow] that all of that is foul of them and an injustice, since it was not a punishment for a prior sin. And if they let that pass [as admissible], it is said to them: then likewise too, [a person's] toiling of himself in the pursuit of knowledge, refinement (al-adab), and the benefits of religion and the world — they must [then hold] him to be in it a wrongdoer toward himself, since it was not a punishment of him for a prior sin. So if they make that obligatory, they have contradicted both the observable and the rational [world] together, since the pursuit of discipline and instruction, and the pursuit of the welfare of religion and the world, stands [established] in the reason of all created beings as something deemed good, which everyone enjoins and desires and does not deem foul.

: Q presses the §2 counterexample into a reductio with two further cases of beneficial undeserved pain: (1) medical pain — cupping (ḥijāma), bloodletting (faṣd), bitter medicine, eye-treatment for ophthalmia (ramad) — and (2) self-imposed toil in the pursuit of ʿilm and adab. Both are universally judged good though painful and non-punitive; so the premise "undeserved pain = injustice" is false by universal consent of al-shāhid wa-l-maʿqūl. The medical examples are concrete and culturally specific (the standard materia of Baghdad medicine), reinforcing that the argument is from common experience, not abstraction.
§4 — The general principle: pain is good when it secures a benefit; God's pain to infants is compensated by Paradise

And if they fall back upon [conceding] that the pains a person brings upon himself and his child in the pursuit of knowledge and refinement are good in reason, even though they are not a punishment upon the one pained by them for a sin of his — it is said to them: then, if that is so, and the pains we have mentioned are not injustice and not foul, what objection have you to its being the case that the rest of the pains by which God pains infants are likewise not injustice, even though they are not a punishment of them?

If they say: those pains we mentioned were allowed to be other-than-punishment, along with their goodness in reason, only because of the benefits in them for the one pained — it is said to them: and what objection have you to its being the case that the pains God brings about upon infants are not a punishment of them, and that He is not a wrongdoer toward them, because of the benefits in them — which are their being compensated for them (taʿwīḍuhum minhā) with the bliss of the Garden (naʿīm al-janna), which is more excellent than all benefits — just as charging [with duty] (al-taklīf) and toiling [under it] was good because of the reward (al-thawāb) attained thereby? For just as the pain involved in being charged [with duty] indicated to us that we are rewarded when we do what we are charged with — and by this indication it became wisdom and justice and went outside the bound of frivolity (al-ʿabath) — likewise the paining of infants indicates the great compensation and benefits they have in that, and by that it goes outside the bound of injustice and frivolity.

: Q now supplies the positive theodicy. Pain is justified — not as desert, but — by benefit: the infant's suffering is offset by taʿwīḍ (compensation), specifically the bliss of Paradise (naʿīm al-janna), "more excellent than all benefits." The structure is explicitly modeled on the Bahshamī account of taklīf (moral obligation): God's imposition of burdensome duty is not ʿabath (purposeless cruelty) but wisdom, because it is the route to thawāb (reward). So too undeserved infant-pain is ḥikma wa-ʿadl, not injustice, because it secures ʿiwaḍ (compensation). The terms taklīf, thawāb, ʿiwaḍ, ʿabath are core Bahshamī theodicy vocabulary (cf. ʿAbd al-Jabbār, al-Mughnī vol. 13 al-Luṭf and the al-aʿwāḍ discussions); compensation for the undeserved pain of children and animals is a signature Bahshamī doctrine.
§5 — Objection: knowledge-pain is good only because unavoidable; God could compensate without pain. Reply: the benefit is a gratuitous favor He may withhold

So if they say: the pains by which knowledge and refinement are attained were good only because we do not arrive [at them] except by that toil; and were it feasible for us to reach that without pain, it would not have been good in our reason to pain ourselves in seeking them — whereas as for the pains God brings about upon infants in order to compensate them by this benefit you have described, can He not deliver it to them without pain? So for that reason it is foul of Him and becomes injustice and frivolity —

it is said to them: His giving them that favor without pain, [a favor] which they do not deserve thereby, is [a matter of] sheer bounty (tafaḍḍul); and the one who shows bounty (al-mutafaḍḍil) has it [in his right] to withhold his bounty. And if that is so, then why is it not admissible for Him to pain them so that they may deserve that compensation — even though He is able to deliver it to them without pain — since, had He not pained them, it would be admissible for Him to withhold from them that great benefit? Tell me: if He were to inform them, while they are intelligent [adults], "I pained you with a slight pain [and] gave you for it a great benefit, which is more than the benefits you seek by toiling yourselves and harming yourselves; and had I not pained you with this slight pain I would not have given you this great benefit, since it was Mine to withhold it from you, as you did not deserve it of Me" —

: The objector concedes pedagogical pain only as a necessary means (we cannot get knowledge otherwise) and presses: God is omnipotent, so He could compensate infants without pain, hence the pain is gratuitous cruelty. Q's reply pivots on tafaḍḍul (gratuitous favor / supererogatory bounty): the Paradise-compensation is not owed; it is tafaḍḍul, and "the bestower of bounty has the right to withhold it" (li-l-mutafaḍḍil an yamnaʿa faḍlahu). Therefore God may attach the unowed favor to a pain-condition (so that the infant comes to deserve the ʿiwaḍ), exactly as a benefactor may set terms on a gift. The section runs into the suspended quotation that §6 completes (the OCR carries the sentence over the p189 page-break without a section marker, as Nemoy's text does). The tafaḍḍul / istiḥqāq (favor / desert) distinction is a load-bearing Bahshamī pair.
§6 — The slight-pain-for-great-benefit choice; and that God may withhold what is not owed

— would it not be admissible in their reason that they should choose this slight pain in order to attain by it this benefit, when they knew that they would not attain it except by this matter? And this stands [established] in the reason of every rational being. And since it is admissible that the rational being should choose this pain for the sake of this benefit, it is admissible that God should choose this pain for them so as to make them attain this benefit, which it was good in reason to choose for its sake; [and] God will [surely] do that for them.

[Section 6 proper:] And if they say: when God is able to give you that without pain, by [His] bounty, and bounty is good in reason, it is not admissible that He withhold from them what He is able to do — it is said: and whence is that obligatory? Is not what God is able to do of bounty without limit, and is not what He has bestowed upon His servants not [the exhaustion of] His power? So there must [always remain further] favors. It is said: is it not, then, admissible that He be able [to bestow] favors which He does not bestow upon His servants when they do not deserve them? So what objection have you to His withholding from them this benefit we asked you about, which they did not deserve of Him without this pain — just as it was His to withhold from them whatever is other than that, since they did not deserve it of Him? Then it is said to them: did not God charge His servants with His obedience so that they might deserve by it His reward, though He is able to make them attain that without charge and without desert? So likewise it is admissible that He make them attain this pain so as to deserve by it this favor, even though He is able to make them attain [it] without pain — there is no difference. So when it is admissible that pain be just in the case of infants and others — in the manner we have made plain — it does not follow that God's paining of infants is a punishment of them by Him.

: §6 completes the suspended "slight-pain-for-great-benefit" argument (the rational adult would freely choose a small pain for a great unattainable-otherwise good; so God may justly impose it), then rebuts the omnipotence-objection a second way: divine bounty is infinite and never exhausted, so there will always be favors God could bestow but does not — withholding an unowed favor is not injustice. The clinching analogy is taklīf itself: God could grant reward gratis but instead instituted moral obligation so that servants deserve it (li-yastaḥiqqū); pain functions identically as the desert-generating condition for ʿiwaḍ. The conclusion retires the root-premise: undeserved infant-pain is ʿadl (just), so it need not be ʿuqūba (punishment) — and the prior-life inference collapses.
§7 — That God begins with pain is not injustice; not every withholder of maximal bounty is a wrongdoer

And they may rely on [the claim] that God's initiating (al-ibtidāʾ) afflictions upon His servants is injustice. So when we have shown them the goodness of afflictions in reason — when the outcome of that issues in a great benefit — they say: would it not [then] have been more excellent, and greater in benefit, and more immense in generosity and bounty, had He given them that without paining them? But this is a departure from their [own] claim that it is injustice — since not everyone who has not been generous with all that he is able to do is a wrongdoer, nor is everyone who has conferred a benefit, [while] able to confer a greater benefit than it, frivolous (ʿābith).

: A neat dilemma-dissolution. The objector retreats from "it is injustice" to the weaker "pain-plus-compensation is less generous than gift-without-pain." Q points out this is no longer the injustice charge at all — it is merely a claim about degrees of generosity. And it fails too: a benefactor who confers a real (if not maximal) benefit is neither a wrongdoer (ẓālim) nor frivolous (ʿābith). The objection has been argued down from a charge of injustice to a non-charge.
§8 — They deny that creation is a present beginning, and that benefits may be unequally distributed at creation

And they may deny that God's creation of these infants — and likewise of the full-grown, and of all the classes of animals — is a beginning (ibtidāʾ) from God now; [they say] rather it must be that He had created them before this present time, on the ground that it is not admissible for God to create any one of His creatures before another or after [another], and that it is not admissible that He create them in differing forms, and not admissible that the favors upon them differ in the beginning of His creating them. They said: because His preferring some of His creation [over others] with what He does not bestow upon another is favoritism (muḥābāh) and an inclination toward caprice (mayl ilā al-hawā); and since that is not admissible of God (mighty and exalted), it is not admissible that He show bounty to some of His servants with what He has not shown to another.

: A subsidiary transmigrationist argument, defending the prior-existence thesis on a distributive-justice ground: if God creates creatures now with unequal endowments (forms, faculties, fortunes), that unequal allotment would be muḥābāh (favoritism) and mayl ilā al-hawā (caprice), which is impossible of God; therefore the inequalities must be deserved — and again the prior life of merit and demerit is invoked to explain present inequality. This is the "problem of natural inequality" arm of the metempsychotic theodicy, parallel to the infant-suffering arm of §1.
§9 — Reply: unequal favor is not favoritism; a giver who gives one more than another wrongs neither

It is said to them: if it were obligatory that His benefiting one [creature] be an inclination toward caprice, it would [equally] be obligatory that His benefiting all creation be an inclination toward caprice. And further: we have not found that the giver, when he gives Zayd a gift and does not give the like of it to ʿAmr, is — in the usage of the people of the language — showing favoritism (muḥābin) to him. Then it is said to them: had God not benefited ʿAmr except with what He benefited Zayd, and made Zayd and him equal — would it not [then] be the case that He had wronged neither of them, nor shown favoritism to the other? When they say "yes," it is said to them: then when He benefits Zayd with more than what He gave him, and does not give the like of this increase to ʿAmr, do you allege that He is a wrongdoer toward ʿAmr and a shower-of-favoritism to Zayd? And how does the increase of benefit become foul of Him when He does it to one of the two and not the other — given your [own] statement that, had He not done it to either of them, that would not have been foul? And how is it not good of Him to withhold from one of them a thing which, had He withheld it from both together, would have been good of Him? Nay — what objection have you to [the proposition] that, when withholding it from both together would have been good, His withholding it from one of them and giving it to the other is [all the] more fit to be good? And in this there is no [room for] distinction; and in it is the invalidation of what they claimed of the difference of forms and benefits, and [the establishment of] the admissibility that infants and the rest of the animals be at the beginning of God's creating them, and that they had not been created before this present time, nor in any abode other than this one.

: Q dismantles the favoritism-argument with an a fortiori. First, a reductio: if unequal benefit is caprice, then equal benefit to all would equally be caprice (since any bestowal is "preference" of the recipient over the non-existent) — absurd. Second, the linguistic-usage point (ahl al-lugha): no one calls a giver who gives Zayd more than ʿAmr a "favoriter." Third, the core a fortiori: since God could justly withhold a benefit from both, He may a fortiori justly give it to one and withhold from the other — withholding from one is a lesser act than withholding from both, which was conceded just. The Zayd/ʿAmr pairing is the standard kalām "two-parties" thought-experiment for testing claims about ẓulm and istiḥqāq. The upshot retires the distributive-inequality arm: present inequality needs no prior-life explanation; creation now, in differing forms, is just.
§10 — May a human strike a child to compensate him? Only when the striker gains; God gains nothing

So if they ask us, saying: is it [then] admissible that one of us strike a child in order to compensate him for that with a compensation? — it is said to them: his striking him is not foul in reason — [if it be] in order to compensate him — provided the striker among us has, in striking him, a benefit, such that he would compensate him with a compensation that discharges this striking or more than it, and provided he is secure that this striking will not [end up] falling upon [the child's] very life; and he has [the right to] do that in reason before the coming of revelation (al-samʿ), even though it is forbidden in the revelation today. But if the striker has, in this striking, no benefit, and there is in it [a benefit] only for the one struck — for what he attains of compensation — then it is foul of the striker; and that is because his giving him the compensation involves a harm upon the giver from among us. For this gift, and the like of it, is good of us only when there is for us in it a benefit: either that one deserves by it a reward from God (mighty and exalted), or that one deserves by it thanks and praise from people, or that the giver gave it not for the benefit of another but out of the tenderness of his heart toward another — so that he repels thereby from himself the burning of the heart and the anxious concern with the affair of the one he gave to. But as for when there falls away from the gift all that we have described of the existence of benefit, and the person's gift of his property is a harm upon him and a diminution of his possession, [then] it is foul of him to harm himself without there being for him in this harm a benefit from one of these aspects we have mentioned.

: Q concedes a hard case — a human may justly inflict pain (strike a child) for the sake of compensating him — but hedges it with conditions that expose the disanalogy with God: (i) the human striker must himself gain (reward from God, praise from people, or relief of his own riqqat al-qalb, tender-heartedness); (ii) the compensation must outweigh the blow; (iii) it must not risk the child's life; and (iv) it was permissible pre-revelation (qabla majīʾ al-samʿ) though now forbidden by sharʿ. Where the human gains nothing and the gift only depletes him, the act is foul — because a needy human harming himself for no gain is irrational. The whole apparatus sets up §11: God, being ghanī (self-sufficient), is under none of these constraints. The ʿaql / samʿ (reason / revelation) distinction — an act foul-or-fair by reason independently of, and sometimes overridden by, revealed law — is a core Bahshamī meta-ethical commitment.
§11 — The Lord of the worlds is not so: He is self-sufficient, gains nothing, loses nothing — so His initiating pain to benefit is good

And this is not the way (sabīl) of the Lord of the worlds (mighty and exalted) in His paining the infant in order to compensate him for it — because He (mighty and exalted) is self-sufficient in Himself (ghanī bi-nafsih): He draws no benefits to Himself, nor repels harms from Himself, nor profits from the thanks of [His] servants nor from their obedience; rather the benefit in that is for them alone. And what He gives them of compensation neither harms Him nor profits Him. For that reason it is good of Him to initiate the pain, in order to benefit thereby the one pained with that for which He compensates him. But as for the human being — since he was poor and needy, and it was not good of him to do an act except to draw thereby a benefit or repel thereby a harm — it is foul of him to pain a child in order to compensate him, since that pain and that compensation bring no benefit upon him, and there is in it [only] harm to himself and diminution of his property.

: The decisive disanalogy and the reason the infant-suffering theodicy works for God but not for a human benefactor. God is ghanī bi-nafsih (self-sufficient in Himself) — He neither gains (lā yajtalib manfaʿa) nor loses (lā yadfaʿ maḍarra) by anything He does for creatures; the benefit accrues to them alone. Hence God may initiate (yabtadiʾ) pain purely for the sufferer's compensatory good, with no self-interested motive — precisely the case that is foul for a needy human (§10), whose every act must serve his own benefit. This ghanī premise is the very premise the transmigrationists used in §1 to argue God cannot be unjust; Q turns it to show God can justly initiate uncompensated-by-desert pain — dissolving their inference that such pain must be punishment for prior sin.
§12 — Total amnesia: the human remembers nothing of any prior abode, though he remembers childhood and recovers memory after sleep and illness

Then the people of metempsychosis (ahl al-tanāsukh) are questioned, and it is said to them: why does the human being not, with the perfection of his intellect in this abode, recollect his being in the abode that was before it? If they say: because of the remoteness of the epoch (buʿd al-ʿahd) — it is said to them: and how is it admissible that he forget because of the remoteness of the epoch, when we see him live a hundred years and more and [still] recollect what he was in during his childhood, while we do not see him recollect anything at all of what you allege he was in before this abode? If they say: death made him forget that — it is said to them: but does not the human being sleep and then awake, and not forget what he was in before sleep? And is his death for a day anything but like his death for a thousand years, and is his sleep for an hour anything but like his sleep for a year? And when death has passed away, why does he not recollect, just as he recollects when sleep has passed away? And besides — how is it admissible that death make him forget, when death does not co-exist with forgetting [in the one who has it]? Tell me: were he to die for a day and then live, becoming intelligent, would he not know what he was in before death? If they say "no," the observable [case] confounds them, namely that the human being may fall ill with a severe illness and sleep for many days, and when he awakes recollects all that he was in before sleep; and likewise, if he die for a day, or ten days, or a year, or a hundred years, and then live, he must recollect what he was in before death. So had the human being been existent [and] intelligent before this abode, he would have recollected that without fail.

: The first empirical disproof: total, exceptionless amnesia of any prior life. Q forecloses the two transmigrationist escapes. (1) "Remoteness of epoch" (buʿd al-ʿahd) fails: a centenarian still recalls his own childhood, yet no one recalls a prior incarnation. (2) "Death erased it" fails on a tight analogy: death is to sleep as a long span is to a short span (sleep does not erase pre-sleep memory; recovery from severe illness with long unconsciousness restores it) — so death-as-transition should likewise leave memory intact, and "death does not co-exist with forgetting" in the revived. The argument is empirical-inductive from al-shāhid (the observable), Q's recurring evidential register, and presses the transmigrationist on the brute fact that the theory predicts recoverable prior-life memory which is universally absent.
§13 — Unremembered punishment is pointless: justice requires the punished know why he is punished

And they are also questioned, and it is said to them: which is the fitter and the more obligatory in reason and wisdom — that the human being be punished for what he did and [that he] know that he is one who recollects what he did [and is] punished for it; or that he be pained and punished while not recollecting what he perpetrated and did, and not knowing that this pain is a punishment of him? If they claim that ignorance of that is the more correct and more obligatory in reason and wisdom, they have brazenly defied the intellects (kābarū al-ʿuqūl) — since there is no dispute among the people of intellect that, for one who has perpetrated a sin, the punishment's befalling him while he recollects it and knows that this punishment befell him for what he did and sinned, is more obligatory and more correct in wisdom than the inflicting of that upon him while he does not recollect and does not know that the cause of that punishment is the occurrence of that sin of his. And if they answer [in accordance] with what we have said, it is said to them: then why did the Wise One (al-Ḥakīm) abandon what is more correct and more obligatory in wisdom and do other than it? And is this anything but a [mere] claim from you, and the falsity (buṭl) of what you incline to of metempsychosis?

: The second disproof, turning the purpose of punishment against the theory. Punishment is rationally pointful only if the punished knows what he is being punished for (deterrence, moral acknowledgment, justice-as-seen). But on transmigration the reborn infant is punished for a sin he cannot recollect and does not know to be the cause — which is the less wise arrangement. Since al-Ḥakīm (the Wise One) does not choose the less-wise over the more-wise, the metempsychotic punishment-scheme imputes folly to God. kābarū al-ʿuqūl ("they brazenly defied the intellects") is Q's standing polemical register for a position that flouts universal rational intuition (cf. al-ḥayārā, glossary §VIII; the same mukābara charge appears against the resurrection-deniers, Bab 8 §2).
§14 — Job and the prophets demand and receive the reason for affliction — yet no one is ever told "for a prior round"

Then it is said to them: inform us about these infants whom He punished in the state of their infancy — had speech and intellect arisen in them at the moment the pain and the afflictions befell them, would they not have [the right] to say to their Creator, "we are infants who have committed no sin; so by what have we deserved that these afflictions should descend upon us, since You are just, doing no wrong, and bringing down no trial save upon one who deserves [it]?" Would not the Creator (mighty and exalted) be bound to answer them and to inform them that this is for what they perpetrated in a round before that round (fī karra qabla tilka al-karra) — just as Job asked, in his saying [Job 13:23] כַּמָּה לִי עֲוֺנוֹת וְחַטָּאות פְּשָׁעַי וַחֲטָאתִי הוֹדִיעֵנִי ("how many are my iniquities and sins? make me know my transgression and my sin"), and his saying [Job 10:2] אֹומַר אֶל אֱלֹוהַ אֶל תַּרְשִׁיעֵנִי הוֹדִיעֵנִי עַל מָה תְרִיבֵנִי ("I will say to God: do not condemn me; make me know why You contend with me"); then he followed that with his saying [Job 3:20] לָמָּה יִתֵּן לְעָמֵל אֹור וְגוֹ' ("why is light given to him that is in misery," etc.)? So by this saying he made plain that whoever is afflicted with a trial, and is not informed why He afflicted him, [the affliction] is ascribed to frivolity (al-ʿabath).

And likewise He relates of the Children of Israel that they asked about a thing of what He ascribed to them, and He answered them and confronted them with their deeds (waqqafahum ʿalā afʿālihim); and that is in His saying [Mal 1:7] וַאֲמַרְתֶּם בַּמָּה גְאַלְנֺוּךָ ("and you said, wherein have we polluted You"), and His saying [Mal 3:8] וַאֲמַרְתֶּם בַּמֶּה קְבַעֲנוּךָ ("and you said, wherein have we robbed You") — so He answered them point by point, and did not bar them from being confronted [with the truth], nor say to them, "it is not for you to ask about what I do," such that it would be feasible for a heretic (mulḥid) to charge [God] with wrong and to cavil. And we have [already] said, in the twelfth bab of this Maqala, that the Creator (exalted be His praise) confronts people in the Hereafter with their wicked deeds when He wishes to punish [them]; and that is in His saying [Amos 4:13] כִּי הִנֵּה יוֹצֵר הָרִים וּבוֹרֵא רוּחַ וּמַגִּיד לְאָדָם מַה שֵּׂחוֹ ("for behold, He who forms the mountains and creates the wind, and declares to man what is his thought"), and His saying — concerning [Ps 22:2] אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי וְגוֹ' ("my God, my God, why have You forsaken me," etc.) — He said [Ps 50:7] שִׁמְעָה עַמִּי וַאֲדַבֵּרָה וְגוֹ' ("hear, my people, and I will speak," etc.), [Ps 50:7] לֹא עַל זְבָחֶיךָ אוֹכִיחֶךָ וְגוֹ' ("not for your sacrifices do I reprove you," etc.), and He said [Ps 50:16] וְלָרָשָׁע אָמַר אֱלֹהִים וְגוֹ' ("but to the wicked God says," etc.) — so He informed him that He confronts him with his deeds, and that is the time of reward and punishment (al-thawāb wa-l-ʿiqāb). And likewise these [infants]: לֹוּ כָאנוּ מֻעָאקַבִין לַוַגַבַּ אֲן יֻוַאקַפוּ עַלַי מַא דַֿא יֻעַאקַבּוּן ("had they been [ones] punished, it would have been obligatory that they be confronted with that for which they are punished"). And this is a clear proof.

: The third and culminating disproof, from prophetic precedent and the structure of just confrontation (muwāqafa). If infant-suffering were retributive (for prior-round sin), then — were the infant articulate — God would owe it the reason ("for what you did in a karra before this karra"). Q grounds the principle that the afflicted are entitled to know why in Job's repeated demand to be told his sin (Job 13:23; 10:2; 3:20 — Job's point being that unexplained affliction would be ʿabath, frivolity), and in God's actual practice of confronting people with their deeds (Mal 1:7; 3:8 — answered "point by point") and reproving them with specified charges (Amos 4:13; Ps 50:7, 16) — cross-referenced to Bab 12 of this Maqala on the eschatological muwāqafa (confrontation at judgment). Since God never confronts the suffering infant with a prior-round sin — no such reason is ever given — the retributive-transmigration reading is excluded: "had they been punished, it would have been obligatory that they be confronted with that for which they are punished." The clinching sentence is preserved in the source in Hebrew script (Judeo-Arabic in Hebrew letters: law kānū muʿāqabīn la-wajaba an yuwāqafū ʿalā mā dhā yuʿāqabūn), as the diff-report confirms; rendered here in transliteration plus translation. muwāqafa is among the eschatology anchor-terms staged in glossary §VI.

- The bab's subject and adversary. The heading is fī al-radd ʿalā man qāla bi-l-tanāsukh — "on refuting whoever professed metempsychosis." The adversaries are not the Christian dualists of Babs 1–7 but al-muwaḥḥida (professors of [divine] unity) who hold transmigration of souls — the current Q announced at the close of Bab 16 ("we now turn to the refutation of those who profess metempsychosis among the ʿĀnānites and others"). Like the resurrection-deniers of Bab 8, this is an intra-monotheist eschatological controversy, and Q deploys the same aṣl / farʿ (root/branch) method: demolish the single root-premise and the branches fall.

- The theodicy of infant suffering is the hinge. The transmigrationists' whole case (§1) is a theodicy: undeserved suffering would be injustice; God cannot be unjust; therefore the suffering is deserved; therefore it was earned in a prior life. Q's strategy is to break premise one — not all undeserved pain is injustice — and he does so with a graded series of counterexamples (§§2-4: a parent's discipline, medical pain, self-imposed study-toil), then with the positive taʿwīḍ (compensation) theodicy (§4): infant-pain is offset by naʿīm al-janna, exactly as the burden of taklīf is offset by thawāb. This is recognizably Bahshamī compensation-theory (the aʿwāḍ owed to children and animals for non-punitive suffering), here put to anti-transmigrationist use.

- The tafaḍḍul / istiḥqāq and ghanī arguments (§§5-11). Against the omnipotence-objection ("God could compensate without pain"), Q argues that the Paradise-benefit is tafaḍḍul (unowed bounty) which God may withhold, and that He may justly attach a desert-generating pain-condition to it (§§5-6); that divine bounty is infinite, so a withheld favor is never injustice (§6); that unequal distribution is not muḥābāh / favoritism (§9, the Zayd/ʿAmr a fortiori); and decisively (§§10-11) that the human-benefactor disanalogy turns on God's being ghanī bi-nafsih — self-sufficient, gaining and losing nothing — so that He, uniquely, may initiate pain purely for the sufferer's compensatory good. Note that ghanī is the transmigrationists' own premise from §1, here turned against their conclusion.

- The three positive disproofs (§§12-14) move from the rational-theodicy refutation to direct attacks on transmigration as fact: (12) amnesia — universal, exceptionless failure to recall any prior life, against the recall of childhood and the recovery of memory after sleep/illness, with the death-is-to-sleep-as-long-is-to-short analogy; (13) pointlessness — unremembered punishment is the less wise arrangement, which al-Ḥakīm would not choose; (14) silence — God's documented practice (Job's demand for his charge; the muwāqafa of Mal 1/3, Amos 4, Ps 50) is to tell the afflicted their sin, yet no infant is ever told "for a prior round," so the suffering is not retributive. §14 cross-references Bab 12 of this Maqala on eschatological confrontation.

- The karra ("round / cycle") vocabulary. Q names the metempsychotic re-incarnation a karra (lit. "turn, recurrence," root k-r-r) — "a round before that round" (karra qabla tilka al-karra, §14). This is his technical term for one cycle of the transmigrating soul through a body; the doctrine itself is al-tanāsukh. The framing of the prior life as one in which the soul was ʿuqalāʾ bālighīn (intelligent and full-grown), accountable and punished by demotion into the present (often lower or suffering) form, is the specific transmigrationist anthropology Q reports.

- The Hebrew-script Judeo-Arabic clincher (§14). The bab's final proposition — law kānū muʿāqabīn la-wajaba an yuwāqafū ʿalā mā dhā yuʿāqabūn — is written in the source in Hebrew letters (Judeo-Arabic, not biblical Hebrew), as the diff-report's p185 rows 27-29 confirm (multimodal recovers it where Kraken garbled it). It is Q's own summarizing sentence, not a citation, and is rendered here in transliteration with translation.
